title: Advanced Train Problems — Two Moving Trains
tagline: Year 3 — Trains crossing each other, overtaking, bridges with moving trains and meeting problems

introduction.overview: Year 2 train problems used a train and a fixed pole or platform, and two trains crossing. Year 3 adds trains that start at different times, meet and then continue, trains that pass a person who is also walking, trains that leave stations at different times, and problems where the lengths and speeds must be recovered from two crossing times. The relative-speed idea and the rule "distance covered = sum of the lengths" are all you need.
introduction.placementRelevance: Advanced train problems are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, typically with two timing facts from which lengths or speeds are found.
introduction.realWorldContext: Rail scheduling, safe overtaking distances and timetable design use these relations.

learningObjectives: Find lengths and speeds from crossing times
Handle trains passing a moving person
Solve meeting problems for trains starting at different times
Compute the time a train takes to pass a platform while another passes it

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: km/h × 5/18 = m/s. Opposite directions: relative speed = sum. Same direction: difference. Crossing: distance = sum of lengths.

coreDefinitions: Crossing: the front of one train meets the front of the other until the rear of the first clears the rear of the second.
Overtaking: the faster train passes the slower in the same direction.
Meeting problem: two trains start from two stations and meet somewhere on the way.
Length from timings: use the same speed to relate two crossing times.
Relative frame: treat one train as stationary and the other as moving at the relative speed.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: A crossing is complete when the relative distance covered equals the sum of the two lengths. Everything else is relative speed in the right direction.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Convert speeds to m/s, decide the direction (sum or difference), write distance = sum of lengths, and divide.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Length from two timings
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: L = S × t₁ (pole) and L + P = S × t₂ (platform)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Meeting trains
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: (1 h late start: subtract the head start)

mainNarrative: For two trains crossing, the relative speed uses the directions. Trains of 120 m and 90 m at 72 and 54 km/h moving opposite cross in (120 + 90) ÷ [(72 + 54) × 5/18] = 210 ÷ 35 = 6 s.
For overtaking, subtract the speeds. A 150 m train at 72 km/h overtakes a 100 m train at 54 km/h in 250 ÷ 5 = 50 s, since 18 km/h = 5 m/s.
Two crossing times give the length. A train crossing a pole in 18 s and a 90 m platform in 27 s has the same speed in both cases: L/18 = (L + 90)/27, so L = 180 m and speed = 10 m/s.

Meeting problems with different start times: a train leaves A at 60 km/h and, one hour later, another leaves B (300 km away) at 40 km/h. After 1 hour the first has covered 60 km. The remaining 240 km closes at 100 km/h in 2.4 h, so they meet 3.4 h after the first started, 204 km from A.
When a train passes a person walking in the same direction, use relative speed. A 100 m train at 54 km/h passes a man walking in the opposite direction at 6 km/h in 100 ÷ (60 × 5/18) = 6 s.

deepDiveAspects.title: After meeting
deepDiveAspects.content: If two trains starting together take t₁ and t₂ hours to reach each other's starting points after meeting, then their speeds are in the ratio √t₂ : √t₁.

deepDiveAspects.title: Equal-length trains
deepDiveAspects.content: If two equal trains of length L cross in time t moving oppositely, the relative speed is 2L/t.

solvedExamples.title: Length from two timings
solvedExamples.question: A train takes 18 s to pass a pole and 27 s to pass a 90 m platform. Find the length of the train and its speed.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The extra 9 s cover the 90 m platform.

solvedExamples.title: Meeting with a late start
solvedExamples.question: A train leaves X for Y at 60 km/h. One hour later another leaves Y for X at 40 km/h. XY = 300 km. How far from X do they meet?

steps.title: First hour
steps.explanation: First train covers 60 km; 240 km remain.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The first train runs 3.4 h in total.

solvedExamples.title: Overtaking
solvedExamples.question: A 150 m train at 72 km/h overtakes a 100 m train at 54 km/h on parallel tracks. How long does it take?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The whole fast train must clear the slow one.

shortcutMethods.title: Sum or difference, sum of lengths

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Draw the positions at each moment.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Relative speed in m/s, distance = sum of lengths, time = distance ÷ speed; for lengths use equal-speed equations.

rulesForApplication: Late start: subtract the head start.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Using full time for both trains.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: A crossing time must exceed either train's own pole time.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Draw two trains and mark the sum of lengths.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Timing facts give equations for lengths.

advanced.question: Trains A and B start together from two stations 300 km apart towards each other. After meeting, A takes 4 h and B takes 9 h to reach the opposite stations. The ratio of speeds A : B is
A train 300 m long passes a platform in 36 s and a pole in 18 s. The length of the platform is (metres)
advanced.explanation: Speed = 300/18 = 50/3 m/s; in 36 s it covers 600 m; platform = 300.

placementStyle.explanation: Head start 40 km. Gain 20 km/h: 2 h after 7 a.m., i.e. 9 a.m.
